abstract: Abstract Background Chronic gingivostomatitis in cats (FCGS) is a moderately to severely painful condition, potentially caused by inadequate immune response to oral antigenic stimulation. Salivary peptidome analysis can identify inflammatory protein mediators and pathways involved in oral mucosal immune activation and may indicate potential therapeutic options for FCGS. Objective Evaluate the diversity and abundance of salivary peptides in cats with FCGS using matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization‐time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry (MALDI‐TOF MS) and nanoscale liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (nano LC‐MS/MS). Animals Thirty‐two cats with FCGS and 18 healthy controls. Methods Case‐control cross‐sectional study. We compared the salivary peptide profiles of diseased and healthy cats. The diagnosis of FCGS was confirmed by histopathology. Saliva samples were analyzed for viral infections using polymerase chain reaction (PCR), peptide mass fingerprint (PMF) using MALDI‐TOF MS, and peptide identification using nano LC‐MS/MS. Results Distinct clusters of peptide profiles were observed between groups. In FCGS, 26 salivary peptides were altered, including apolipoprotein A1, nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group I member 3, fibrinogen alpha chain, interleukin 2 receptor gamma, interleukin 23 receptor, hemoglobin subunit alpha, and serpin peptidase inhibitor clade A (alpha‐1 antiproteinase, antitrypsin) member 12, protein‐tyrosine‐phosphatase, and cholinergic receptor nicotinic alpha 10 subunit. Protein‐anti‐inflammatory drug interaction networks were observed. Conclusions and Clinical Importance Peptide mass fingerprint and peptide profiles identified distinct clusters between FCGS and healthy cats. The 9 novel salivary peptide markers were associated with the JAK/STAT and PI3K/Akt pathways and immune responses. These potentially noninvasive biomarkers may facilitate understanding of FCGS pathophysiology and guide future therapeutic research.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1
Animals and sampling
Saliva samples were collected from 2 groups of cats: 32 cats with FCGS (aged 3‐14 years) and 18 control (CTRL) cats (aged 7‐14 years). All cats underwent comprehensive health assessments, including blood testing, parasite checks, and vaccination records. Inclusion criteria for the CTRL group required the absence of caudal stomatitis and systemic illness, a CBC, serum biochemistry panel, and no evidence of severe periodontitis. For the FCGS group, cats had to have gingivitis, stomatitis, caudal mucositis, no systemic illness, and normal serum biochemistry except for hyperproteinemia and hyperglobulinemia, which are common in cats with FCGS.
1
All cats in the study were evaluated for FIV, FeLV, FHV‐1, and FCV using PCR.
19
,
20
Saliva was collected as previously described.
13
Medications were stopped 7 days before surgery. On the day of surgery, the cats' mouths were cleaned with sterile saline, and the cats were fasted for 6 to 8 hours. Saliva samples were obtained from cats with complete dentition, under anesthesia before dental procedures, without mechanical or chemical stimulation. No premedication was administered, and general anesthesia was induced using propofol (Propofol‐Lipuro, 10 mg/mL, B. Braun Melsungen AG, Germany) at an initial dose of 1 mg/kg, titrated to effect for tracheal intubation. Anesthesia was maintained using isoflurane (IsoVet, Piramal Healthcare, United Kingdom) in oxygen during salivary collection. Whole saliva, approximately 0.5 to 1.0 mL, was collected using a sterile cotton swab for 5 to 10 minutes. Each sample was centrifuged at 4500 rpm for 15 minutes at 4°C to separate cells and debris. The supernatant was mixed with protease inhibitor cocktails and stored at −20°C until analysis, which included peptidomic analysis and molecular testing for FeLV, FIV, FHV‐1, and FCV. Total protein concentrations in salivary supernatants were assessed using Lowry's assay.
21
All experimental protocols were approved by the Mahidol University Animal Care and Use Committee, Thailand (MUVS‐2022‐04‐24). All procedures were performed according to approved guidelines and regulations, and samples were obtained with the informed consent of the cats' owners.
2.2
Histopathology
Mucosal tissue samples were collected from CTRL and FCGS‐affected cats under general anesthesia, specifically from the area lateral to the palatoglossal folds, using iris scissors. Tissue biopsy samples were collected from macroscopically affected mucosa for subsequent histological examination. Biopsies were conducted on all subjects in the FCGS group, targeting the most pathologic regions situated caudally.

2.4
Proteomic analysis for cluster analysis and identification of candidate peptides
2.4.1
MALDI‐TOF MS
Saliva peptides (0.2 μg/μL) were prepared as previously reported.
13
The solution was directly applied to the MALDI steel target plate (MTP 384 ground steel, JEOL, Japan). Eight replicates were used in turn to prevent sample preparation bias. After air‐drying, mass spectra were obtained using JMS‐S3000 SpiralTOF‐plus 2.0 set to linear positive mode with a mass range of 1000 to 6000 Da. Five hundred shots were collected using a 50‐Hz laser for each sample. The mass spectra were analyzed using msTornado Analysis version 1.15. The results of MALDI‐TOF MS were expressed as PMFs and using partial least squares‐discriminant analysis (PLS‐DA). External calibrations were performed using the Proteomass Peptide & Protein MALDI MS calibration kit (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA).
The distribution of peptide profiles of control cats and cats with FCGS into distinct clusters was evaluated. All of the spectra were subjected to hierarchical clustering analyses using Sartorius Stedim Data Analytics' prediction engine (SIMCA). Partial least squares‐discriminant analysis (PLS‐DA) with spectra with 8 replicates was performed for each cat in each group. The distinct samples were excluded from PLS‐DA plots. To confirm the peptide profiles in each group, saliva samples from each group were pooled for MS analysis. Mass spectra of pooled saliva peptides were analyzed as described above.
2.4.2
NanoLC
‐
MS
/
MS
From each sample, 5 μg of peptides were reduced using a disulfide‐containing compound and cysteine residues. Subsequently, the samples were incubated in darkness at 25°C for 45 minutes, dissolved using 0.1% formic acid, and assessed by nanoLC‐MS/MS.
The peptide samples were prepared for injection into an Ultimate 3000 Nano/Capillary LC System (Thermo Scientific, UK) connected to a ZenoTOF 7600 mass spectrometer (SCIEX, Framingham, MA, USA). Briefly, 1 μL of peptides was enriched using a μ‐Precolumn (300 μm i.d. × 5 mm) packed with C18 Pepmap 100 (5 μm, 100 A; Thermo Scientific, UK) and separated on a 75 μm i.d. × 15 cm column packed with Acclaim PepMap RSLC C18 (2 μm, 100 Å) using nanoViper technology (Thermo Scientific, UK). The C18 column was enclosed within a temperature‐controlled column oven set to 60°C. Solvents A and B, which contained 0.1% formic acid in water and 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile, respectively, were used for the analytical column. Solvent B, with a gradient ranging from 5% to 55%, was used to elute the peptides, maintaining a constant flow rate of 0.30 μL/minute for 30 minutes.
For the ZenoTOF 7600 system, the source and gas parameters were configured as follows: The ion source gas 1 at 8 pounds per square inch (psi); curtain gas at 35 psi; collisionally activated dissociation gas at 7 psi; source temperature at 200°C; positive polarity; and spray voltage at 3300 V. For data‐dependent acquisition (DDA), the 60 highest abundance precursor ions were selected from MS1 scans for MS/MS analysis, with an intensity threshold >150 counts per second (cps). Precursor ions were dynamically excluded for 12 seconds after 2 MS/MS sampling, with dynamic capillary electrophoresis‐mass spectrometry (CE) enabled for MS/MS. The MS2 spectra were acquired in the 100 to 1800 m/z range, with a 50‐ms accumulation time, and the Zeno trap was activated. The collision energy parameters included a declustering potential (DP) of 80 V, with no DP and CE spread. A total of 8 time bins were summed with all channels enabled, and the Zeno trap threshold was set to 150 000 cps. The cycle time for the top 60 precursor ions from DDA was set to 3.0 seconds.
2.5
Bioinformatics and statistical analysis
MaxQuant version 2.2.0.0 was used for protein quantification within individual samples using the Andromeda search engine to match MS/MS spectra with the Uniprot
Felis catus
database.
23
Label‐free quantification was performed using standard parameters, allowing a maximum of 2 missed cleavages, 0.6 Da mass tolerance for the primary search, cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification, and methionine oxidation and protein N‐terminus acetylation as variable modifications. Protein identification required peptides with a minimum of 7 amino acids and at least 1 unique peptide. To be included in subsequent data analysis, proteins had to be identified by at least 2 peptides, 1 of which was unique. A protein false discovery rate of 1% was applied, estimated using the reversed search sequences, and a maximum number of 5 modifications per peptide was allowed. The search was performed using a FASTA file containing the
Felis catus
proteome downloaded from UniProt on October 16, 2023.
Multivariate analysis, which included PLS‐DA plots, and univariate analysis, which included a volcano plot, were performed using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 (
http://www.metaboanalyst.ca
).
24
In comparisons of the volcano plot, peptides were deemed significantly altered if they met all of the following criteria: a raw
P
‐value <.05 and a fold‐change (FC) >2.0 or <0.67. The proteins identified from the candidate peptides underwent further investigation using “Stitch EMBL” (accessible at “
http://stitch.embl.de
”) accessed on January 12, 2024 to explore their functions and protein‐protein interactions.
25
Pathway analysis was performed using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database to investigate protein interactions with nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids, including meloxicam, robenacoxib, and prednisolone, within the context of other drugs used to treat FCGS, including interferon‐omega (IFN‐ω), cyclosporine, and oclacitinib.

INTRODUCTION
Chronic gingivostomatitis in cats (FCGS) or lymphoplasmacytic stomatitis is a severe, immune‐mediated, oral mucosal inflammatory disease.
1
Affected cats experience moderate to severe pain and exhibit clinical signs such as halitosis, anorexia, weight loss, and abnormal behavior.
2
,
3
The cause of FCGS is unknown but may be related to an altered immune response to oral antigenic stimulation caused by feline calicivirus (FCV), herpesvirus (FHV‐1), leukemia virus (FeLV), immunodeficiency virus (FIV), and
Bartonella
, as well as noninfectious factors, such dental problems, environmental stress, and hypersensitivity.
4
,
5
,
6
A study performed quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on oral tissues and discovered increased mRNA expression of various toll‐like receptors and proinflammatory genes, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (
TNFA
), interferon gamma (
IFNG
), interleukin 1 beta (
IL1B
), and interleukin 6 (
IL6
).
7
These findings indicate the complex nature of the etiopathogenesis of FCGS, making it an intriguing area of investigation. Another study found an association between esophagitis and FCGS and confirmed inflammation and metaplasia in esophageal tissues by histopathology.
8
The hypothesis proposes that the pathogenic oral microbiota of FCGS‐afflicted cats may be transmitted to the esophagus through saliva. Transmission could induce the release of proinflammatory cytokines, potentially contributing to the development of esophagitis.
8
Thus, salivary analysis may offer an alternative method for investigating the inflammatory protein mediators and pathways involved in oral mucosal immune activation, as well as represent a promising avenue of research on FCGS treatment.
Saliva directly contacts oral lesions and transports serum components from glandular tissue.
9
Saliva is a valuable, noninvasive, and cost‐effective alternative to traditional diagnostic methods such as blood samples or tissue biopsy.
9
It contains diverse proteins, DNA, RNA, metabolites, and microflora, which can serve as biomarkers for early disease detection and personalized treatments, making it an excellent choice for diagnosing both local and systemic diseases.
10
,
11
In the era of ‐omics, matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization‐time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry (MALDI‐TOF MS) and liquid chromatography‐tandem MS (LC‐MS/MS) can accurately identify peptides and proteins that may be associated with diseases.
12
,
13
,
14
Salivary peptidomic and proteomic profiles in dogs with several conditions, including infections, noninfectious disorders, and malignancies, have been reported.
13
,
15
,
16
,
17
The proteomic profiles of feline adipose tissue‐derived mesenchymal stem cell exosomes (fAd‐MSCs) differ between healthy and calicivirus‐positive cats with FCGS, indicating that immune‐mediated diseases such as FCGS with calicivirus may be analyzed by ‐omics.
18
Use of salivary peptidomic profiling in cats is limited in the veterinary field.
We employed untargeted proteomic approaches using 2 methods: MALDI‐TOF MS to compare peptide mass fingerprints (PMF) for detecting differences between healthy cats and those with FCGS for viral detection and histopathology, and nano LC‐MS/MS to analyze the amino acid sequences of peptides based on mass‐to‐charge ratio (m/z). These techniques were utilized to investigate salivary inflammatory peptides, protein mediators, and pathways associated with FCGS. Thus, we investigated the utility of saliva peptidomic profiling for identifying inflammatory mediators as biomarkers in cats with FCGS using MALDI‐TOF MS and nano LC‐MS/MS. Our results enhance the current understanding of disease pathophysiology, provide a foundation for further research on mechanisms of action and therapeutic applications, and facilitate the identification of predictive biomarkers and potency assays for FCGS treatment.

Histopathological results
In FCGS, the reported duration of clinical signs was >6 months. Oral inflammatory lesions were observed in the left and right caudal buccal mucosa (Figure
1A
). All biopsy specimens showed severe inflammation, denoted by a marked infiltration of plasma cells and lymphocytes into the gingival mucosa. Neutrophil infiltration was observed in 50% of the cases. Furthermore, Mott cells, characterized as B lymphocytes containing immunoglobulins, were commonly observed (Figure
1B
). Gingival hyperplasia with no inflammation was observed in the CTRL group (Figure
1C,D
).

The functions of candidate peptides, including their involvement in disease pathophysiology, pathogenesis, and mechanisms of action were explored to identify prognostic biomarkers and potency assays for cats that received treatment for FCGS. Nineteen upregulated proteins and 7 downregulated proteins identified in the FCGS group were analyzed for their interactions with NSAIDs, such as meloxicam and robenacoxib, prednisolone, interferon omega (IFN‐ω; accessed on January 12, 2024), cyclosporine, and oclacitinib (accessed on August 13, 2024), using Stitch EMBL. Seven upregulated proteins were identified in protein‐protein and protein‐chemical interaction networks involving NSAIDs and prednisolone: apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), fibrinogen alpha chain (FGA), hemoglobin subunit alpha (HBA), interleukin 2 receptor gamma (IL2RG), interleukin 23 receptor (IL23R), nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group I member 3 (NR1I3), and serpin peptidase inhibitor clade A (alpha‐1 antiproteinase, antitrypsin) member 12 (SERPINA12). Among these, APOA1, FGA, IL2RG, and IL23R exhibited the highest relationship levels in the protein interaction network (edge confidence >0.9) with functional partners, such as coagulation factor II (thrombin; F2), fibrinogen gamma polypeptide (FGG), IL2, interleukin 2 receptor beta (IL2RB), IL4, interleukin 4 receptor (IL4R), janus kinase 1 (JAK1), and lecithin‐cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). Hemoglobin subunit alpha (HBA), NR1I3, and SERPINA12 showed moderate correlations in protein‐chemical interaction networks (edge confidence >0.4) with ammonia, arachidonic acid, calcium ions (Figure
4A
), and prednisolone (Figure
4B
). Six proteins with increased levels in FCGS were isolated from the networks, including calmodulin‐regulated spectrin‐associated protein family member 2 (CAMSAP2), centrosomal protein 85 kDa (CEP85), 60S ribosomal protein L13 (RPL13), Src homology 2 domains containing E (SHE), solute carrier family 34 (sodium phosphate) member 3 (SLC34A3), and transmembrane protein 164 (TMEM164). The relationships between IFN‐ω, cyclosporine, oclacitinib, and the overexpression of 6 proteins (APOA1, HBA, FGA, IL2RG, IL23R, and SERPINA12) within protein‐protein and protein‐chemical interaction networks are shown in Figure
4C‐E
. Of these, APOA1, FGA, IL2RG, and IL23R exhibited the highest levels of relationships in the protein interaction network (edge confidence >0.9) with functional partners, such as F2, FGG, IL2, interleukin 2 receptor alpha (IL2RA), IL2RB, IL4, IL4R, IL15, JAK1, and LCAT. In contrast, HBA and SERPINA12 were moderately correlated with calcium ions in protein‐chemical interaction networks (edge confidence >0.4). Seven proteins with increased levels in FCGS were identified within these networks: CAMSAP2, CEP85, NR1I3, RPL13, SHE, SLC34A3, and TMEM164. These proteins may play crucial roles in numerous pathways of cancer metastasis, as shown in KEGG pathway maps, namely, the Janus kinase/signal transducers and activators of transcription (JAK‐STAT) signaling pathway, complement and coagulation cascades, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), cytokine‐cytokine receptor interaction, measles, platelet activation, phosphatidylinositol 3‐kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K‐Akt) signaling pathway, and allograft rejection (Table
S3
).

DISCUSSION
We categorized saliva samples into the FCGS or CTRL group based on the typical oral lesions and histological findings indicative of FCGS.
2
,
27
We performed PCR/RT‐PCR to investigate the viral agents associated with FCGS and evaluate the viral infection status in both groups. Previous studies have demonstrated continuous FCV shedding in most cats with FCGS, corroborating prevalence patterns previously reported.
3
,
28
Although no direct causal relationship between FCV and FCGS has been established, various experiments indicate otherwise.
4
,
29
In our study, the frequency of FCV was significantly higher in the FCGS group compared with the control group (
P
= .03). Two controlled studies found no link between FHV‐1 and FCGS.
30
,
31
Previous studies have not clearly linked FeLV and FIV to FCGS.
32
Phenotypically, FeLV‐positive cats exhibit significantly fewer proliferative stomatitis and resorptive lesions but are more prone to develop ulcerative lesions on the tongue.
33
In a study of 60 cats with FCGS, 7% were positive for FeLV and 8% were positive for FIV.
34
In our study, the frequencies of FeLV and FIV were 9.38% and 9.38%, respectively, in 32 cats with FCGS. A recent study on shedding of active calicivirus in cats with FCGS found no association between FeLV, FIV, or herpesvirus and FCGS.
35
Our findings indicate that cats infected with FCV (43.75%) may be more prone to developing FCGS (
P
= .03). However, the proteomic data indicated no correlation between viral detection and the development of FCGS.
We found distinct patterns of peptides in saliva, known as salivary PMFs, between the FCGS and CTRL groups using MALDI‐TOF MS. Both FCGS and CTRL groups exhibited consistent patterns within their respective groups. These patterns included similarities among noninfected cats, cats infected with a single type of virus, and cats infected with multiple viruses. Our findings indicate that changes in salivary peptide profiles may be linked to the inflammatory and ulcerative processes affecting the oral mucosa. The saliva samples of FCGS had distinct peptide profiles related to typical oral lesions and histological characteristics using MALDI‐TOF MS. Previous studies have emphasized the potential of MALDI‐TOF MS profiling as a noninvasive, cost‐effective method for the rapid screening of a large population.
36
This technique has been applied in human medicine to investigate various oral conditions, such as tooth decay, orthodontic tooth movement, periodontal disease, oral cancer, and oral lichen planus.
37
,
38
,
39
Similarly, in veterinary medicine, salivary analysis has uncovered specific peptide patterns associated with oral tumors in dogs, as well as in tissues and serum samples.
12
,
13
,
14
Our results established MALDI‐TOF MS as a rapid and reliable method for identifying FCGS. This technique specifically identified the salivary PMF associated with FCGS, independent of viral detection. Thus, MALDI‐TOF MS potentially could facilitate the diagnosis and detection of disease recurrence. However, additional data from individual patients are necessary to establish comprehensive databases of salivary PMFs and perform statistical analyses of various diseases.
We performed LC‐MS/MS with in‐solution digestion to identify novel peptides and proteins in saliva from cats to understand FCGS better and identify salivary biomarkers with potential for clinical application. We found that APOA1, NR1I3, FGA, IL2RG, IL23R, HBA, and SERPINA12 were overexpressed in FCGS. These proteins interact and respond to medications such as meloxicam, robenacoxib, prednisolone, IFN‐ω, cyclosporine, and oclacitinib. However, no interaction was detected between NR1I3 and IFN‐ω, cyclosporine, or oclacitinib. Functional analysis identified involvement of these proteins in inflammatory pathways, particularly the JAK‐STAT signaling pathway, complement and coagulation cascades, cytokine‐cytokine receptor interaction, platelet activation, and the PI3K‐Akt signaling pathway. These findings align with a previous study showing that the transcriptomic profile of oral mucosal tissues in cats with FCGS is enriched with genes and pathways related to the immune response and inflammation, primarily influenced by IL‐6.
40
These include key pathways such as NF‐κB, JAK/STAT, IL‐17, and type I and II interferons.
40
Additionally, transcriptomic analysis of caudal oral mucosal swabs from cats with FCGS identified significant induction of disease‐associated pathways, including PI3K/AKT signaling and SAPK/JNK signaling, which were altered after treatments such as tooth extraction and mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy.
41
It is likely that the salivary proteins reflect the mRNA expression observed in both oral mucosal swabs and tissues in cats with FCGS. Apolipoprotein A1, the main protein in high‐density lipoprotein, regulates cholesterol and immune responses, inhibits dendritic cell maturation, and is associated with inflammation in conditions such as osteoarthritis, as shown by increased concentrations of markers such as IL‐6 and MMP‐3.
42
,
43
Apolipoprotein A2 (APOA2) or NR1I3, which is an important protein in lipid metabolism, exerts immunosuppressive effects and exhibits increased expression in mammary carcinoma in cats.
44
Investigation into the immunosuppressive mechanism of APOA2 identified its ability to mitigate mammary carcinoma in cats by decreasing IFN‐γ production in CD4+ T cells.
45
In patients with allergic rhinitis, APOA1 and APOA2 concentrations in nasal mucus are significantly increased, indicating their anti‐inflammatory function in the pulmonary epithelium.
46
In FCGS, the mucosa exhibits lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with abundant CD8+ T cells, B cells, and mast cells in the gingiva.
27
Both APOA1 and APOA2 upregulation in FCGS may correspond with imbalances in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
27
,
47
Fibrinogen alpha chain, which is involved in blood coagulation and inflammation, is an acute phase protein marker.
48
Its increased expression in FCGS indicates local oral mucosal inflammation. Similar associations of FCGS with APOA1, FGA, and inflammatory markers have been observed in the synovial fluid of patients with osteoarthritis.
43
,
49
In FCGS, we observed increased APOA1 and FGA concentrations in saliva, which may signify a local inflammatory process in the oral mucosa in response to alveolar bone loss.
50
Chronic gingivostomatitis in cats may be involved in pathways related to inflammation, chondrocyte migration, osteophyte formation, and cartilage degeneration such as osteoarthritis. Furthermore, FCGS tissues exhibit increased expression of IL‐6 and enrichment of the JAK‐STAT signaling pathway, corroborating previous findings. Thus, APOA1, APOA2, and FGA are potential markers for inflammation in FCGS.
40
The highly soluble IL‐2R is likely produced from the enzymatic cleavage of the cell surface membrane IL‐2Rα.
51
Although the functional effects of soluble IL‐2R are debated, proposed mechanisms include IL‐2 sequestration, localized inflammation regulation, and interaction with membrane IL‐2 receptors, which activates the JAK‐STAT signaling pathway.
52
,
53
Interleukin 23 receptor (IL‐23R) signaling modulates intestinal regulatory T cells (Tregs) by affecting cell turnover, suppression antagonism, and cholesterol efflux, potentially exacerbating chronic inflammation in patients with IBD.
54
,
55
Furthermore, the complex association of IL‐23R with JAK family members Jak2 and Tyk2 predominantly promotes STAT3 phosphorylation, linking the JAK‐STAT pathway to IL‐23‐mediated responses.
56
Therefore, IL2RG and IL23R are crucial in immune signaling, with IL2RG overexpression potentially linked to the JAK‐STAT pathway in FCGS. Our study suggests that salivary analysis using proteomic techniques could emerge as a useful diagnostic tool in FCGS research. This comprehensive investigation of inflammatory protein mediators and immune activation pathways within the oral mucosa is intended to advance the proteomic profiling of saliva in cats with FCGS. We identified candidate peptides and pathways, offering insights that will inform future investigations into innovative clinical solutions for FCGS. Furthermore, we performed salivary analysis by PCR/RT‐PCR to evaluate common viral infectious agents of cats, such as FCV, FeLV, FIV, and FHV‐1. This analysis may identify potential causative factors for the immune response observed in cats with FCGS. Further research should evaluate the increased concentrations of APOA1, NR1I3 or APOA2, FGA, IL2RG, and IL‐23R in saliva, which are associated with the JAK‐STAT signaling pathway, in cats with FCGS. Increased HBA and SERPINA12 concentrations indicate their roles in decreasing oxidative stress and exerting anti‐inflammatory effects via the PI3K‐Akt pathway, which may uncover potential targets for managing inflammation in FCGS. Furthermore, low concentrations of PTPs and CHRNA10 may signify altered immune responses. These findings emphasize the potential for targeted therapeutic strategies in FCGS, warranting further investigation. To our knowledge, ours is the first investigation of saliva proteomics in FCGS.
In conclusion, we have provided insight into potential salivary biomarkers and the possible etiopathogenic mechanisms of FCGS. Despite limitations such as small sample size and variations because of concurrent viral infections, our findings emphasize the potential of salivary peptidomics in small animal clinical research. These results lay the groundwork for future studies, but validation using authentic standards and larger cohorts is necessary to confirm the accuracy of these biomarkers. This research also sets the stage for longitudinal studies to track disease progression and treatment responses, which will be crucial in understanding FCGS pathology and therapeutic outcomes. Further research is needed to validate these findings and explore how peptide profiles change over time. Notably, our study focused exclusively on peptides.
